Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. Thank you for taking a few minutes to talk with me today.

I’d like to use a short, well-trusted tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of ten questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling during the past week so we can be sure you’re getting the right support in these early weeks of motherhood.

Everything you share stays confidential between you and your care team. My goal is to create a safe, judgment-free space where you can be completely honest—there are no “right” or “wrong” answers, only what’s true for you. If any question feels difficult, just let me know and we can take it at your pace.

When you’re ready, I’ll ask the first of ten questions. We’ll keep them conversational, and I’ll jot down your answers so we can review them together at the end.

Shall we begin?

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things—would you say you’ve enjoyed a good laugh most of the time, now and then, hardly ever, or not at all?

Most of the time, actually. I still laugh when my husband makes silly faces at the baby, or when the dog tries to “help” during tummy-time. I guess I’ve been able to find those little funny moments almost every day.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, like I said, I’m still laughing—especially when the baby does those tiny hiccup sounds or when my mom tries to sing lullabies off-key. It’s not constant, but it’s definitely there every day.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Most of the time I do. I still get excited about little stuff—like our morning walks to the coffee shop or the new show my best friend and I stream together during naptime. There are moments I feel too tired to plan anything big, but I still find myself looking forward to the small things each day.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Hardly ever. If the baby spits up a ton or won’t settle, I figure it’s just part of the newborn deal—not something I did wrong. I might think “maybe I could have burped him longer,” but I don’t sit there beating myself up about it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little, but not much. Sometimes I’ll suddenly check if he’s breathing in the middle of the night, or worry that a tiny rash means something awful, but the feeling passes once I look at him or call the pediatrician. It’s not every day, and it doesn’t take over.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

No, not really. I haven’t had that kind of sudden scared or panicky feeling. If I get startled, it’s usually because the baby made a weird noise and I jump up to check on him—but it’s not a real panic thing, just new-mom reflexes.
Things have been getting on top of me

Only occasionally. Some days the laundry piles up or the baby won’t nap anywhere but on me, and I feel a little swamped. It passes once my husband gets home or I get a shower in, but every now and then I do think, “Whoa, this is a lot.”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not at all. Once I’m actually in bed, I sleep pretty solidly—well, as solidly as the baby lets me. I might wake up for feeds, but I drift right back off. I haven’t lain there feeling unhappy or wired.
I have felt sad or miserable

Hardly ever. I get a bit weepy maybe once every week or so—usually when I’m overtired—but it’s over in a few minutes and then I’m back to normal. I wouldn’t call it feeling truly sad or miserable, just a moment of “ugh, I’m exhausted.”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, not really. I think I teared up once this week when a lullaby came on and I was already running on four hours of sleep, but it lasted like thirty seconds. I haven’t had any real crying spells.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
Never. That hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 5: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]  Source: Patient self-report via 10-item EPDS-style questionnaire

Symptoms endorsed  
- Occasional fleeting worry about infant safety; resolves with reassurance  
- Mild, situational “overwhelm” when baby will not nap or chores accumulate; remits with support  
- Rare (<1×/wk) brief tearfulness when fatigued; no sustained low mood

Symptoms denied  
- Persistent sadness, anhedonia, guilt, self-blame, panic attacks, sleep-onset or maintenance problems related to mood, crying spells, self-harm ideation

Pattern  
Overall affective tone is positive; daily enjoyment and laughter reported. No clusters consistent with major depressive or anxiety pathology.

Screening significance  
Current responses place patient well below conventional cut-offs for postpartum depression or generalized anxiety on standard screening tools. No safety concerns identified. Continue routine postpartum monitoring; re-screen if clinical picture changes.
